enrichment.short_title: EIA challenge to Imperial Wharf outline planning permission

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Assessment of Environmental Effects) Regulations 1988

key_facts: Burkett challenged outline planning permission for the large Imperial Wharf mixed-use development at Fulham granted by Hammersmith and Fulham LBC.
The House of Lords had remitted the case after holding the original JR application was not out of time.
Grounds attacked the adequacy of the environmental statement, reserved matters for design and stage 3 siting, traffic, contamination and publicity of revised information.
The court found the authority had lawfully assessed environmental information and substantially complied with regulation 4(2).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive judicial review in the High Court following remittal by the House of Lords on time limits.
enrichment.outcome: Application for judicial review dismissed; leave to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where outline permission is granted, an authority may reserve design and limited siting matters if likely significant environmental effects have been assessed at the permission stage; a failure to state expressly in the decision that environmental information was considered may be cured by substantial compliance where the statutory purpose was met and no prejudice is shown.
legal_issues: Whether reserved matters for design, landscaping and stage 3 siting prevented compliance with Schedule 3 of the 1988 EIA Regulations
Whether traffic and contamination impacts were adequately assessed
Whether revised environmental information required fresh publicity
Whether regulation 4(2) required an express statement in the planning decision

enrichment.short_title: Intractable contact dispute resolved by section 37 care route
key_facts: Two children ceased all contact with their father after the resident mother falsely persuaded them he and his parents had abused them.
Wall J invited the local authority under section 37 to consider care proceedings and assessment under an interim care order.
Assessment showed significant harm in the mother's care; contact with the father was restored.
The court ultimately made a residence order to the father with a two-year supervision order and mother contact at the authority's discretion.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Published twin judgments in private law Children Act proceedings following a section 37 investigation and interim care order.
enrichment.outcome: Residence order to the father; two-year supervision order to the local authority; mother's contact in the authority's discretion.
enrichment.ratio: An intractable contact dispute caused by a resident parent's unfounded alienation may properly be resolved by a section 37 direction leading to care proceedings and assessment, with final orders transferring residence where significant harm in the resident parent's care is established.
legal_issues: Whether section 37 was an appropriate route to assess and remedy intractable contact refusal
Whether the children were suffering significant harm in the mother's care
What final welfare orders should follow restoration of contact with the father

confidence.notes: Two published judgments with clear welfare outcome; parties anonymised in case name.

enrichment.short_title: Dyson transparent vacuum bin trade mark appeal
key_facts: Dyson sought to register marks consisting of a transparent collection bin on its bagless vacuum cleaners.
The Registrar refused registration under sections 3(1)(a)-(c) for lack of distinctiveness and descriptiveness.
Survey evidence showed consumers associated clear bins with Dyson but not necessarily as a badge of origin by 1996.
The hearing officer's decision was upheld on review; acquired distinctiveness was referred to the ECJ.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the High Court from a Trade Marks Registry hearing officer decision refusing registration.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on inherent distinctiveness and descriptiveness; question on acquired distinctiveness referred to the Court of Justice.
enrichment.ratio: A transparent collection chamber that indicates a bagless cleaner is exclusively descriptive under section 3(1)(c) and lacks inherent distinctiveness under section 3(1)(b); appeals from ex parte registry decisions are normally by way of review rather than full re-hearing.
legal_issues: Whether the appeal should proceed by review or re-hearing
Whether the clear bin mark is descriptive of bagless cleaners
Whether the mark has inherent or acquired distinctiveness
Whether functionality objections may be raised under section 3(1)(c)

enrichment.short_title: Non-domestic rates liability orders quashed for invalid service

statutes_considered.title: Non-Domestic Rating (Collection and Enforcement) (Local Lists) Regulations 1989

key_facts: Pilot Foods Ltd was made liable by magistrates for over £100,000 in non-domestic rates for premises it leased but did not occupy.
Delta Project Management and later Rosecrown Restaurants occupied the restaurant premises under operating agreements.
Summonses were served at 23 Villiers Street rather than the company's registered office at 29 Villiers Street.
The company only learned of the liability orders in February 2002 and Westminster City Council did not contest the claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of two magistrates' court liability orders made without effective notice to the company.
enrichment.outcome: Liability orders quashed; Westminster City Council ordered to pay costs assessed at £5,000.
enrichment.ratio: Service of a non-domestic rates summons at the rated premises rather than a company's registered office breaches regulation 13(2) and denies natural justice; where the company was not in rateable occupation, liability orders made in its absence must be quashed.
legal_issues: Whether summons service complied with the 1989 Regulations
Whether failure to serve denied the company a fair hearing
Whether the company was in rateable occupation
Appropriateness of judicial review despite delay

enrichment.short_title: Freezing order discharged for without-notice disclosure breaches
key_facts: HM Customs & Excise alleged Arena Corporation and Mr Schroeder diverted bonded alcohol to the UK black market without paying duty and VAT.
Peter Smith J granted without-notice freezing orders in December 2002 which Arena sought to continue until trial.
HMCE's supporting evidence contained serious failures to disclose material favourable to Schroeder and misstatements.
Morritt J refused to continue the orders despite a prima facie fraud case.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to continue Mareva/freezing orders obtained without notice against the defendant in alleged excise diversion fraud proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Freezing orders not continued until trial; golden rule breach held to require discharge despite prima facie fraud.
enrichment.ratio: Serious breaches of the duty of full and frank disclosure on a without-notice freezing order application are penal in nature and may require refusal to continue the order even where the claimant has established a prima facie case of fraud.
legal_issues: Whether HMCE breached the golden rule on the without-notice application
Whether breaches were serious enough to refuse continuation
Whether a fresh injunction with costs penalties was an adequate sanction
Proportionality between fraud enforcement and disclosure duties

enrichment.short_title: Journalist intermediary ordered to identify Brady records source
key_facts: Ian Brady's confidential PACIS clinical notes from Ashworth Hospital were leaked to the Daily Mirror during his 1999 hunger strike.
MGN was ordered in earlier proceedings to disclose its source; Ackroyd was identified as the intermediary.
Ackroyd argued his case differed because sources acted in the public interest and were not paid.
Gray J granted summary judgment requiring disclosure; the Court of Appeal allowed Ackroyd's appeal for trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against summary judgment requiring investigative journalist Robin Ackroyd to identify the hospital employee who supplied Ian Brady's clinical notes.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; summary judgment set aside and matter remitted for trial.
enrichment.ratio: Protection of journalistic sources is a constant public interest under section 10 and Article 10, but a journalist may have a real prospect of resisting Norwich Pharmacal disclosure where his personal investigative history and unpaid public-interest sources materially distinguish his case from earlier litigation against the publisher.
legal_issues: Whether Ackroyd was bound by the MGN/House of Lords decision
Whether the hospital source had a public interest defence to breach of confidence
Whether non-payment of sources altered the section 10 balancing exercise
Whether medical records confidentiality automatically overrides source protection at summary stage

enrichment.short_title: Custody time limit extension quashed in drug conspiracy case
key_facts: Four defendants faced a 4-6 week Crown Court trial for conspiracy to supply class A drugs based on undercover purchases and video evidence.
Judge Tonking refused to extend custody time limits because prosecution video disclosure was late and causative of delay.
Judge Chapman later extended limits after the trial date slipped, misunderstanding Tonking's findings as limited to a five-day delay.
Custody time limits had expired by the time Maurice Kay J heard the judicial review on the eve of trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of HHJ Chapman's decision extending custody time limits after an earlier refusal by HHJ Tonking.
enrichment.outcome: Extension decision quashed; defendants entitled to bail as of right with conditions; trial to proceed on bail.
enrichment.ratio: A later Crown Court judge may not lawfully extend custody time limits by mischaracterising an earlier refusal and without investigating whether earlier listing would have been possible but for prosecution failures to serve crucial video evidence with due diligence.
legal_issues: Whether the prosecution acted with due diligence and expedition
Whether prosecution delay caused the need for extension
Whether Judge Chapman could revisit Judge Tonking's findings
Whether relief remained available after custody time limits expired

enrichment.short_title: Reinsurance aggregation of Kuwait and BA aircraft war losses
key_facts: On 2 August 1990 Iraq captured Kuwait International Airport, plundering Kuwait Airways aircraft and spares while a stranded BA Boeing 747 remained on the ground.
KAC fleet losses were held to arise from one event—the invasion and capture of the airport.
The BA aircraft was destroyed by coalition bombing in February 1991 after a wait-and-see period.
Reinsurers argued the BA loss did not aggregate with KAC losses under the excess-of-loss 'one event' clause.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Commercial Court judgment on aggregation of war-related aviation losses under a whole-account excess-of-loss reinsurance.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; loss of the BA aircraft held not to arise from the same event as the KAC fleet losses.
enrichment.ratio: Under an 'arising from one event' aggregation clause, losses require a significant causal link to a single unifying event; the BA aircraft's later destruction in the Gulf War was a separate event from the invasion-led immediate loss of the KAC fleet despite the shared starting point of airport capture.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'arising from one event' in excess-of-loss reinsurance
Whether BA aircraft loss related back to 2 August 1990 deprivation
Application of the unities test to immediate and delayed total losses
Whether destruction in war or invasion was the operative event

enrichment.short_title: Child support enforcement and Article 6 access to court
key_facts: Mary K sought a declaration that the Child Support Act 1991 was incompatible with Article 6 because a parent with care cannot enforce maintenance assessments personally.
She had applied for maintenance in 1993 but the Agency delayed processing and enforcement for years.
The claimant was not on benefit and argued the State had no sufficient interest to monopolise enforcement.
The court held Article 6 was engaged but the scheme was HRA-compliant when combined with judicial review and section 7 damages.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review seeking a declaration of incompatibility under section 4 HRA 1998 and further relief for Agency delay after 2 October 2000.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration of incompatibility refused; separate HRA damages claim on delay remitted for case management.
enrichment.ratio: A parent with care has an autonomous civil right to child maintenance and Article 6 is engaged by the statutory bar on personal enforcement, but the Child Support scheme remains HRA-compliant because judicial review plus a section 7 damages action gives full jurisdiction to remedy unreasonable enforcement failures.
legal_issues: Whether Article 6 applies to enforcement of child support assessments
Whether section 8 prevents access to court in breach of Article 6
Whether the scheme is saved by Alconbury/Begum principles
Whether Agency delay after HRA commencement gives rise to damages

enrichment.short_title: Juror's letter disclosing deliberations held contempt
key_facts: Mr Scotcher was the sole dissenting juror in a 2000 wounding and affray trial convicted 10-1.
He wrote anonymously to the defendant's mother detailing jury votes, arguments and alleged pressure to convict without evidence.
He had been warned by jury literature and a video that disclosing deliberations was contempt punishable by imprisonment.
He later admitted authorship, arguing a miscarriage-of-justice motive should excuse disclosure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's application for committal for breach of section 8(1) Contempt of Court Act 1981.
enrichment.outcome: Contempt established; no miscarriage-of-justice exception to section 8 accepted.
enrichment.ratio: Section 8(1) absolutely prohibits disclosure of jury deliberations and votes; a juror's genuine belief that a verdict was unsafe does not create an implied exception, because jury secrecy protects candour, finality and jurors themselves and is compatible with Article 6.
legal_issues: Construction of section 8(1) Contempt of Court Act 1981
Whether a miscarriage-of-justice motive creates an exception
Compatibility of jury secrecy with Article 6 and Article 10
Proper channel for juror concerns about verdict safety
